summary: The Gemara analyzes bar Kappara's citation of R. Meir about wood added from the sides of the altar, discusses whether that wood is valid for the altar fire, and then addresses which mitzvot override Shabbat and which override the prohibition of offering in a state of ritual impurity.

display.whats: What does bar Kappara teach in R. Meir's name, and does the wood added from the sides of the altar count as a valid arrangement?
display.hint: Bar Kappara taught: R. Meir would say that wood added from the sides of the altar (not from the main arrangements) is not counted as a distinct arrangement. The Gemara then pivots to the question of which prohibitions are overridden by the Temple service and which are not.
display.title: Wood From the Sides Doesn't Count, and Who Overrides Shabbat

learning.ahaMoment: Communal public offerings override Shabbat and communal tumah. Individual offerings and certain other prohibitions are not overridden. The distinction is between 'tzibur' (communal) and 'yachid' (individual).
learning.memoryAnchor: Bar Kappara teaching R. Meir: wood from the sides of the altar is not a valid arrangement.
learning.learnerQuestion: Does wood placed on the sides of the altar count as a valid arrangement, and which Temple services are permitted to override Shabbat and ritual impurity?
learning.coreTension: Bar Kappara cites R. Meir that wood from the altar's sides is not counted as a valid arrangement, and the Gemara must explain what this teaches beyond what was already known, before turning to the broader question of which prohibitions communal Temple service may override.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara clarifies that wood placed on the sides (not the designated arrangement positions) does not count, and establishes the broader principle that communal public offerings override Shabbat and communal ritual impurity, while individual offerings do not.

takeaway.text: Wood placed on the sides of the altar, rather than the designated arrangement positions, is not counted as a valid arrangement; communal public offerings override Shabbat and ritual impurity, but individual offerings do not.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the override of Shabbat and impurity applies to any Temple offering, missing that the Gemara restricts it specifically to communal (tzibur) offerings, not individual (yachid) ones.

misconceptions.correction: The override applies specifically to communal public offerings, such as the tamid and musaf - individual offerings do not override Shabbat or ritual impurity.

quizSeeds.answer: No. Only communal public offerings (like the tamid and musaf) override Shabbat and communal ritual impurity.

sugyot.finalRuling: Wood from the sides of the altar is not a valid arrangement; communal offerings override Shabbat and tumah; private offerings do not.

Ritual impurity - certain forms are overridden by communal Temple service needs.

rashiTranslations.en: Rashi: 'but from this side' - he did not begin from this side, even though it is the western side; this is how the text should be read.
Rashi: 'Rabbi Meir would say: the limbs of the burnt-offering that were left over' - we do not read this as 'the weekday burnt-offering.'
Rashi: for if we read it that way, the Gemara's challenge 'we have already learned this' would make no sense; rather this comes to teach about Shabbat.
Rashi: and if you object that the Mishna's 'every day' already includes Shabbat, note that the Gemara raises this as a further challenge.
Rashi: the Gemara goes on to raise yet another difficulty concerning Shabbat specifically, showing these are separate points.
Rashi: 'what is bar Kappara teaching us' - since he says one makes an arrangement for these leftover limbs.
Rashi: on a weekday, we have already learned this from the Mishna's own statement about the four arrangements.
Rashi: every day there were four arrangements, and one of them was designated for limbs that were left over.
Rashi: 'for disqualified offerings' means those parts that, once they went up onto the altar, are not brought back down.
Rashi: 'once the fire took hold of them' - from that moment they are considered accepted, the bread of the altar.
Rashi: continues explaining the significance of the fire taking hold for the offering's validity.
Rashi: 'we have learned: today there are five' refers to the five arrangements taught for Yom Kippur.
Rashi: since Yom Kippur is treated like Shabbat in stringency, and the Mishna teaches about the eve-of-Yom-Kippur daily offering's limbs.
Rashi: one makes an arrangement for those limbs on Yom Kippur itself.
Rashi: 'every day' - the Mishna teaches there were four arrangements, and this phrase includes even Shabbat by implication.
Rashi: continues explaining why 'every day' must be read to include Shabbat in this context.
Rashi: 'and this disagrees with Rav Huna' - meaning it disagrees with bar Kappara's position as well.
Rashi: moreover it disagrees with the claim that 'every day' in the Mishna precisely includes Shabbat.
Rashi: for Rav Huna holds that 'every day' means every day except Shabbat.
Rashi: 'its beginning overrides Shabbat' - the Shabbat daily-offering is slaughtered on Shabbat itself.
Rashi: and it is offered on Shabbat as well, since its beginning stage overrides the Shabbat prohibition.
Rashi: 'its end does not override Shabbat' - meaning the completion stage does not carry the same override.
Rashi: the limbs of the Friday daily-offering are not burned once it becomes dark into Shabbat.
Rashi: rather, he brings those limbs up onto the altar while it is still day, before Shabbat begins.
Rashi: this is how the text should be read: 'the matter itself, Rav Huna said, etc.'
Rashi: 'what does it mean that it does not override' - the Gemara asks what specifically is not overridden.
Rashi: it does not override the law of impurity for the burning of the fats and sacrificial portions.
Rashi: rather, the override applies only to the sprinkling of the blood alone.
Rashi: another version reads the terms differently: 'its beginning' means the burning of the fats.
Rashi: and 'its end' means the limbs that were left over from the evening before.
Rashi: this is the version I heard, but the first version seems more correct to me.
Rashi: 'impurity' - opens the next clause, continuing onto the following daf.
